strengths: Addresses a realistic and underexplored problem setting in personalized federated learning (PFL) by jointly tackling data heterogeneity (distinct multi-modal tasks with distribution shifts) and model heterogeneity (different architectures/hidden dimensions/depths across clients), moving beyond simplistic non-i.i.d. splits or same-architecture LoRA-rank variations used in prior work.

Introduces DRAKE, a comprehensive and carefully curated multi-modal FL benchmark spanning 40 tasks from 19 datasets, with task heterogeneity, temporal distribution shifts, and unseen-task evaluation splits, which fills a clear gap relative to existing FL benchmarks (well documented in Table 1).

Technically well-grounded contributions: SIMA uses decayed gradient similarity for customized aggregation, and PQ-LoRA introduces dimension-invariant P/Q modules with rigorous theoretical backing (Theorem 1 on maximal span under orthogonality, Theorem 2 proving zero aggregation error when freezing A/B), plus practical solutions for depth/weight misalignment (block-wise aggregation, MSE/CCA alignment).

Extensive empirical validation across multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-LLM, Fed-Aya), multiple model families (LLaMA3, Qwen2.5), homogeneous and heterogeneous setups, and various ablations (rank r, NB, weight alignment, SIMA variants), showing consistent improvements in both personalization ("Self") and generalization ("Others").

Thorough analysis of computational/memory overhead (Table 10) showing the method incurs only modest additional cost (~5-10%) compared to SFT, and per-client breakdowns that provide nuanced interpretation of where gains are concentrated.
Strong reproducibility documentation: detailed algorithms (pseudocode), hyperparameters, benchmark construction details, and a full NeurIPS checklist.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a maximum of 10 clients (acknowledged as a limitation), which is far from the scale of real-world federated deployments and leaves open how SIMA's pairwise similarity computation and PQ-LoRA alignment scale with many more clients or many more distinct architectures.

The DRAKE benchmark, while comprehensive, is a re-curation/re-splitting of existing public datasets rather than newly collected data, and the degree of realism in modeling actual real-world non-i.i.d. and streaming distributions (vs. an engineered task-based split) could be discussed more critically.

Average performance gains over strong baselines are sometimes modest (e.g., 1-3% in several settings), and per-client tables show that for some clients (e.g., Client 8 in Tab.16, Client 2/9 in Tab.16) FedMosaic underperforms SFT, suggesting the benefit is uneven and dependent on task/client composition, which is not deeply analyzed (e.g., what characterizes clients where PFL helps vs. hurts).

The block-wise aggregation and weight alignment mechanism in PQ-LoRA rely on assumptions (approximately linear layer correspondence via CKA, shared public pretraining data for alignment) that may not hold for more diverse architecture families beyond the LLaMA/Qwen decoder-only backbones tested; scalability of alignment to many heterogeneous architectures (not just pairs) is only briefly mentioned as extendable without full empirical validation for >2 distinct model types at scale.

Some baseline combinations are somewhat ad hoc (e.g., combining non-heterogeneous-aware PFL baselines with Fed-ET to handle heterogeneous models), which could bias comparisons in FedMosaic's favor since these baselines were not originally designed for this integration.
Code is not released at submission time, limiting immediate reproducibility verification despite thorough documentation.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and practically relevant problem: jointly handling data heterogeneity (distinct multi-modal tasks per client) and model heterogeneity (different architectures/sizes per client) in personalized federated learning, rather than the simplified single-dataset non-i.i.d. splits used by most prior work.

DRAKE benchmark aggregates a wide range of existing multi-modal datasets (40 tasks, 19 sources) into a more realistic FL testbed with task heterogeneity, temporal distribution shifts, and held-out generalization splits, which is a useful (if largely curatorial) contribution to the community.

Provides theoretical justification (Theorems 1 and 2) for design choices such as freezing A/B in PQ-LoRA and orthogonal initialization, along with block-wise CKA analysis supporting the layer-alignment strategy.

Extensive experimental coverage: multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-LLM, Fed-Aya), multiple heterogeneous architecture families (Llama-3, Qwen2.5), homogeneous vs. heterogeneous setups, computational/memory cost comparisons, and numerous ablations reported in the appendix.
weaknesses: Reported gains over the strongest baselines are frequently marginal (often 1-3 points in Alast/AAUC) relative to the substantial added complexity of the method (dual adapters, SIMA gradient tracking, PQ-LoRA with CCA/MSE alignment, orthogonality post-processing, block-wise aggregation, learnable gating), raising concerns about whether the complexity is justified by the empirical benefit.

PQ-LoRA's cross-architecture alignment procedure requires access to a 'public' dataset drawn from the pretraining corpora of the employed MLLMs; relying on such data to align heterogeneous adapters partially undercuts the privacy motivation central to the federated learning framing, and its availability/representativeness in real deployments is not well justified.

The client-model-assignment protocol (Sec. A.3) assigns each client's architecture based on oracle SFT performance measured in advance for every candidate model size on that client's task — this is an unrealistic, circular procedure that would not be available in a genuine deployment and undermines the paper's stated goal of reflecting real-world heterogeneity.

Block-wise aggregation and layer alignment are justified only via CKA similarity within closely related model families (Llama-3 variants, Qwen-2.5 variants, and their cross-family combination); it is unclear whether the near-linear alignment assumption holds for more structurally divergent architectures (different depths/width ratios, different vision encoders, non-transformer backbones), limiting the generality claimed in the introduction.

Some theoretical results are close to definitional (e.g., Theorem 2's proof that freezing A and B makes the 'ideal' and 'practical' aggregate identical is essentially a tautology) and add limited insight beyond motivating the freezing design choice already adopted for practical reasons.

Ablation studies (e.g., SIMA gradient variants in Table 20, weight-alignment variants in Table 21) show small effect sizes with overlapping standard deviations, making it hard to conclude that each individual design choice is empirically well-supported rather than incidental.

The evaluation relies on custom, non-standard accuracy metrics (token-overlap-based accuracy for open-ended VQA, GPT-4 scoring for Fed-Aya) without validation against established automatic metrics, and all baselines are adapted via combination with Fed-ET, raising questions about whether comparisons are fully fair to methods not originally designed for this exact heterogeneous LoRA setting.

No code or data is released at submission time (promised only after publication), which combined with the pipeline's many interacting components (alignment, orthogonalization, block assignment, EMA gradients) raises practical reproducibility concerns despite the detailed pseudocode in the appendix.

DRAKE, while extensive, is a repackaging of existing public datasets rather than newly collected data, and its distribution-shift/task assignments per client appear to be manually curated design choices without a principled justification for why the particular partitioning best reflects 'real-world' heterogeneity.

strengths: Introduces DRAKE, a comprehensive and realistic multi-modal PFL benchmark with 40 diverse tasks spanning VQA, visual relation, and multi-modal reasoning, including distribution shifts and unseen-task evaluation splits, which is a valuable community resource beyond simplistic non-i.i.d. label-skew benchmarks.

Proposes two well-motivated and theoretically grounded components: SIMA for similarity-aware aggregation (backed by intuitive gradient-based task similarity with EMA decay) and PQ-LoRA for dimension-invariant knowledge sharing across heterogeneous architectures, supported by formal proofs (Theorem 1 on maximal span, Theorem 2 on zero aggregation error).

Extensive empirical validation across multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-LLM, Fed-Aya), multiple heterogeneous model families (LLaVA-Llama3, LLaVA-Qwen2.5) with 2-3 different scales, and both PFL-Static/-Dynamic settings, consistently showing improvements over many strong baselines (DITTO, FedSim, FedIT, TAKFL, FedDPA, FedDAT, PerAda, FedMKT).

Thorough ablations (SIMA gradient variants, PQ-LoRA rank, weight alignment, number of blocks) and a careful computational/memory overhead analysis showing the method adds minimal cost (~5-10%) relative to SFT while achieving better personalization/generalization trade-offs.

Strong analysis of per-client behavior clarifying when PFL helps vs. when SFT suffices, plus fast-adaptation experiments on unseen tasks demonstrating practical benefits of the learned global knowledge.
weaknesses: The scale of federated experiments is limited to at most 10 clients due to computational constraints, which is modest relative to real-world FL deployments and is acknowledged as a limitation.

The overall average performance gains over baselines are sometimes relatively small (e.g., 1-3% in some 'Self' metrics), requiring per-client breakdowns to appreciate where the method helps most, which could raise questions about robustness of the average improvements.

The full pipeline (SIMA gradient tracking, PQ-LoRA block-wise alignment via MSE + CCA + orthogonality projection) is fairly complex with many hyperparameters (temperature τ, EMA rate α, regularization λ, block count NB), which may complicate practical adoption and reproducibility despite detailed appendix algorithms.
Code is not released at submission time (promised after publication), limiting immediate verifiability of the many implementation details.
Block-wise aggregation and the CKA-based near-linear layer alignment assumption may not generalize well to architectures with more divergent designs than the tested Llama/Qwen families.

strengths: Addresses a realistic and underexplored combination of data and model heterogeneity in PFL, filling a genuine gap versus prior simplified setups.
DRAKE benchmark is comprehensive (40 tasks, 19 datasets, multi-image support, temporal shifts, unseen-task evaluation) and clearly differentiated from prior FL benchmarks.

Extensive empirical evaluation across many heterogeneity configurations (same-family, cross-family, large-scale 52-client LLM setting, text-only benchmarks), with detailed cost analyses and a large ablation suite.
Reasonable theoretical grounding: proofs for zero aggregation error when freezing A/B, and orthogonality argument maximizing PQ-LoRA's representational capacity.

Consistent improvements over many strong/recent baselines across most settings, with per-client analysis showing where and why gains occur, plus fast-adaptation results supporting generalization claims.
weaknesses: Justification for using a shared frozen proxy model (Ws) to estimate task relevance across heterogeneous local models is largely heuristic/empirical rather than theoretically grounded.

Privacy claims (sanitized gradients via EMA/noise/subsampling) are asserted but not rigorously verified with formal DP guarantees or empirical privacy-attack evaluation, despite privacy being central to the paper's motivation.

Absolute performance gains over the strongest baselines are sometimes small, and baseline rankings are not fully consistent across tables (e.g., FedDAT's relative performance varies), raising questions about robustness of claimed improvements.

PQ-LoRA alignment depends on public data whose domain match to client data affects performance, and requires pairwise alignment across heterogeneous architecture types, which may raise scalability concerns as architectural diversity grows.

DRAKE's task heterogeneity is constructed via heuristic re-splitting/relabeling (keywords, GPT categorization) of existing datasets, and the realism of these splits as proxies for genuine personalization heterogeneity is not deeply validated.

The manuscript is extremely dense with a very large appendix, making it hard to verify core claims without extensive cross-referencing, and some fairness details of baseline tuning are only briefly addressed.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely under-explored combination of problems (simultaneous data and model heterogeneity) in personalized federated learning for multi-modal LLMs, and provides a large experimental matrix (homogeneous/heterogeneous, static/dynamic, cross-family, LLM-only) to probe it.

DRAKE is a reasonably large and diverse multi-modal FL benchmark (40 tasks, 19 source datasets, unseen-task splits) that is more realistic than prior single-dataset non-i.i.d. splits used in FL literature.

The paper provides theoretical support (Theorems 1 and 2) for the design choice of freezing A/B and only sharing P/Q in PQ-LoRA, along with an extensive ablation and hyperparameter-sensitivity study in the appendix.
Computation/communication overhead analysis is included and shows the method is not dramatically more expensive than SFT, which is a relevant practical consideration.
weaknesses: The reported personalization ('Self') gains over SFT are often small (often 1-3 Alast points, and sometimes within noise given the reported standard deviations), which is a weak empirical signal given the substantial added system complexity (dual adapters, gradient EMA/noise/compression pipeline, CCA/L2 weight alignment, orthogonality post-processing, block-wise layer matching).

Several published PFL/FD baselines underperform plain SFT by large margins in the main tables (e.g., DITTO, PerAda, FedMKT below SFT on 'Self' in Table 2/3), which is surprising for methods explicitly designed for personalization and raises concerns about whether baselines were adequately tuned or fairly adapted to this new heterogeneous setting (the paper itself admits baselines were 'combined' with Fed-ET or modified, which could handicap them).

The privacy argument for RELA (transmitting EMA-decayed, noised, and subsampled last-layer gradients of a frozen auxiliary model to the server) is asserted via citations rather than empirically validated (e.g., no gradient-inversion attack experiments), so the practical privacy benefit over standard FL weight sharing is unproven.

The theoretical contributions (Theorems 1 and 2) are fairly elementary linear-algebra facts (maximal span of an outer-product space under orthogonal frozen factors; zero aggregation error when A/B are shared and frozen) and do not provide deep insight beyond motivating the engineering design.

PQ-LoRA's cross-architecture alignment procedure requires access to a public dataset resembling client data distributions and must be re-run for every pair of heterogeneous architectures before federated training even begins, which is a nontrivial practical assumption, particularly in a cross-silo setting where public data availability or domain match cannot be guaranteed in general.

DRAKE's task construction (grouping existing academic VQA/reasoning datasets into client-specific task bundles, partitioning by keyword/GPT-based categories) is a reasonable but still largely synthetic heterogeneity simulation rather than genuine naturally-arising user data, limiting the claim of 'real-world' task heterogeneity.

The method introduces many additional hyperparameters (τ, α, Ns, μ, λ, NB, gradient frequency f) each requiring its own sensitivity study to justify a single fixed setting used across very different benchmarks, which raises concerns about generalizability of the chosen defaults to unseen deployment scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: jointly handling data AND model heterogeneity in personalized federated learning for multi-modal LLMs, moving beyond simplified LoRA-rank-only heterogeneity or single-dataset non-iid splits used in prior work.

DRAKE benchmark is a substantial and useful contribution: 40 tasks from 19 datasets spanning VQA, visual relation, and multi-modal reasoning, with temporal distribution shifts and an unseen-task split for generalization evaluation, filling a clear gap versus existing FL benchmarks (well documented in Tab. 1 comparison).

PQ-LoRA is a clean, well-motivated technical contribution: freezing A/B after alignment and only sharing dimension-invariant P/Q modules enables cross-architecture (cross-depth, cross-hidden-dim) knowledge sharing with theoretical backing (Theorem 1 on span maximization, Theorem 2 on zero aggregation error) and favorable compute/communication cost analysis.

RELA (relevance-guided aggregation via sanitized, EMA-decayed gradient similarity) is a reasonable, privacy-conscious mechanism for mitigating task interference during aggregation, with ablations isolating the benefit of decay and frozen-model gradients versus simpler alternatives.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons against 8 PFL baselines across multiple benchmarks (DRAKE, HFLB, Fed-Scope, Fed-Aya, Fed-LLM-Large), multiple heterogeneity configurations (2-model, 3-model, cross-family Llama/Qwen), homogeneous vs. heterogeneous settings, scaling to 52 clients, and consistent outperformance in both personalization and generalization metrics.

Very thorough ablations and sensitivity analyses in the appendix (hyperparameters, public data choice/size, block count NB, rank r, temperature, noise scale, gradient sampling ratio, weight alignment components, client model assignment robustness) demonstrate the method is not fragile to design choices.

Reasonably transparent cost analysis showing modest computational (~9.8%) and communication (net reduction) overhead relative to SFT/FedAvg baselines, which is important for practical federated deployment claims.
weaknesses: The gains in average 'Self' accuracy are often modest (1-3 points) and per-client analysis reveals substantial heterogeneity in benefit, with the paper's own explanation (SFT already near-optimal for 'easy' tasks) being somewhat post-hoc; a more principled discussion of when/why PFL helps would strengthen the claims.

RELA's privacy claims rely on gradient compression, noise injection, and EMA-mixing as heuristic defenses against gradient inversion, but no formal privacy guarantee (e.g., differential privacy budget) is provided, leaving the privacy argument somewhat informal despite being used to motivate design choices.

The theoretical results (Theorems 1 and 2) are somewhat narrow in scope (idealized assumptions such as Q=0, exact orthogonality, identical A/B across clients) and mainly justify design choices already intuitive from model-merging literature (frozen shared backbone avoids aggregation conflict); their practical significance beyond motivating the freezing strategy is limited.

Block-wise aggregation and weight alignment rely on approximately linear CKA correspondence between models of different depths, which may not generalize well to architectures with very different designs beyond Llama/Qwen decoder-only transformers (e.g., encoder-decoder, mixture-of-experts); limited discussion of failure cases.

Client-task assignment and model-to-client assignment in experiments appear to be curated/favorable (choosing model sizes based on SFT performance in Sec A.3), which could be seen as an idealized rather than fully 'realistic' heterogeneous setup, somewhat undercutting the paper's framing around realism.

The large number of hyperparameters (temperature, EMA ratio, noise scale, sampling ratio, NB, λ, rank r) introduced by combining RELA and PQ-LoRA increases the practical complexity and tuning burden for deployment, even though the paper shows reasonable robustness across a range of values.

Some comparisons (e.g., against MTL methods, similarity-aware aggregation baselines) are relegated entirely to the appendix and could be more central given their relevance to assessing RELA's novelty relative to existing aggregation strategies.
